author: reek
body: The cell is a mailbox, not a queue, and that is deliberate. A key struck while the machine is busy -- generating a keypair, hashing the seed -- is dropped rather than replayed into whatever screen appears next. Buffering type-ahead across a screen boundary would let a stray keystroke pre-fill a passphrase field, or a stray Enter confirm a verdict nobody read. During a prompt the consumer polls in a constant-stack loop that allocates nothing, so it never falls behind a human hand.

author: reek
body: The read and the clear are one instruction. atomic-exchange compiles to XCHG against memory, which asserts LOCK on x86 whether or not the prefix is written, so the keyboard ISR cannot land between the read and the clear and have its scancode zeroed. A plain peek-then-poke loses a key in that window. The window is two instructions wide and no test would ever catch it.

author: reek
body: The exchange is 64 bits and the ISR stores the scancode zero-extended to 64, so the low byte is the whole answer; masking keeps gk-take total no matter who else has written the cell.
